title: Krishna and the Pandavas Break the Chaityaka Peak
story:
They had come to Girivraja to humble the pride of Jarasandha, and they began by breaking a mountain.

Krishna showed Arjuna the capital of Magadha standing in all its beauty — filled with flocks and herds, its stock of water never exhausted, adorned with fine mansions in excellent array, free from every kind of calamity. Five large hills protected the city of Girivraja: Vaihara, Varaha, Vrishava, Rishigiri, and the delightful Chaitya, all of high peaks, overgrown with tall trees of cool shade, and connected with one another, their slopes concealed by forests of delightful and fragrant Lodhra trees covered with flowers. It was here that the illustrious Gautama of rigid vows had begotten Kakshivat and other celebrated sons, and here that the mighty monarchs of Anga and Vanga and other countries had come in olden times to Gautama's abode and passed their days in joy. Owning such a delightful and impregnable city, Krishna said, Jarasandha was ever bent on seeking the fruition of his purposes, unlike other monarchs. "We shall, however, by slaying him today," he said, "humble his pride."

They entered the city of Magadha and approached Girivraja, full of cheerful and well-fed inhabitants belonging to all four orders, where festivities were perennial. And on arriving at the gate of the city, the brothers — instead of passing through it — began to pierce the heart of the high Chaityaka peak, the hill worshipped by the race of Vrihadratha and by the citizens, the hill that delighted the hearts of all the Magadhas.

There, long ago, Vrihadratha had slain a cannibal called Rishava, and from the monster's hide he had made three drums and placed them in his own city — drums of such making that once beaten, their sound lasted a full month. It was at that point, where those drums covered with celestial flowers used to yield their continuous sound, that the brothers broke the Chaityaka peak down. Attacking with their mighty arms that immovable, huge, high, and old and celebrated peak, always worshipped with perfumes and floral wreaths, those heroes broke it down. And desirous of slaying Jarasandha, they seemed by that act to place their feet upon the head of their foe. With joyful hearts they entered the city.

But the city read the omen before it saw the men. The learned Brahmanas residing within Girivraja saw many evil omens and reported them to Jarasandha. The king's priest made him mount an elephant and whirled lighted brands about him; and Jarasandha, possessed of great prowess, with a view to warding off those evils, entered upon the celebration of a sacrifice with proper vows and fasts. The sacred hill of his ancestors had fallen at his gate, and all his rites could not undo what the portents promised.

Meanwhile the brothers — unarmed, or rather with their bare arms as their only weapons — entered the capital in the guise of Brahmanas. They beheld the extraordinary beauty of the shops, full of various edibles and floral wreaths, supplied with articles of every variety that man can desire. Those best of men, Krishna, Bhima, and Arjuna, passed along the public road, and, endued with great strength, snatched forcibly from the flower-vendors the garlands they had exposed for sale. Attired in robes of various colours, decked in garlands and ear-rings, the heroes entered the abode of Jarasandha like Himalayan lions eyeing cattle-folds. Their arms, besmeared with sandal paste, looked like the trunks of sala trees. The people of Magadha, beholding those heroes looking like elephants, with necks broad like those of trees and wide chests, began to wonder much.

Those bulls among men passed through three gates crowded with men, and proudly and cheerfully approached the king. And Jarasandha, rising up in haste, received them with water to wash their feet, with honey and the other ingredients of the Arghya, with gifts of kine, and with other forms of respect. "Ye are welcome," the great king said. And both Arjuna and Bhima remained silent at this.

The welcome hung in the air unanswered. Two of the three guests had said nothing at all, and the king of Magadha stood waiting amid the honours he had just given them.
reflection: The broken peak was the first move of the whole enterprise, and it was deliberate: a king's own sacred hill, torn down at his gate, announced that these strangers had not come to beg but to humble him. The omens the priests read afterwards only told the city, in another language, what its own eyes had already seen.
next_story_tease: The silence of the two disguised brothers would need an explanation.
hero_scene: Krishna, Bhima, and Arjuna, disguised as Brahmanas, tearing down the great Chaityaka peak at the gate of Girivraja with their bare arms, while the sacred hill — garlanded and worshipped — crashes down around the drum-shrine where its music used to sound.

Krishna, Bhima, and Arjuna breaking the peak with bare arms
the three drums of Rishava's hide, covered with celestial flowers
the priests reading omens and Jarasandha's sacrifice with lighted brands
the trio passing the flower-vendors' shops and snatching garlands
